title: Nutrition and cognitive achievement: An evaluation of the School Breakfast Program
effect_size: availability of SBP increases standardized test scores ('increases student achievement'); magnitude ≈ +0.02–0.1 SD per program introduction (paper reports gains comparable to a modest fraction of the free/reduced lunch gap)
basis_of_estimate: fuzzy regression discontinuity on state adoption mandates

title: Food insufficiency and American school-aged children's cognitive, academic, and psychosocial development
input_modified: food insecurity (moving from food-insecure to sufficient)
outputs: arithmetic scores, grade repetition, school suspensions, psychosocial
effect_size: food-insufficient 6-11y: significantly lower arithmetic scores, ~higher risk of grade repetition & seeing a psychologist (ORs typically 1.5-2+ after adjusting for poverty)

title: Food insecurity in children: impact on diet quality and academic achievement
effect_size: FOI children scored significantly lower with 76% FI prevalence in study sample (single-school)

title: Public Housing, Housing Vouchers, and Student Achievement: Evidence from Public Housing Demolitions in Chicago
effect_size: ≈0 effect: children from demolished high-rise public housing do no better or worse than peers

title: Housing Vouchers and Crime Trends: Experimental Evidence (Jacob & Ludwig, Milwaukee MTO-like)
effect_size: mixed: voucher receipt raised adult crime & reduced juvenile delinquency in Milwaukee lottery study (voucher families less constrained on neighborhood choice, not forced moves)

title: Effects of eviction moratoria on health/related (vs. eviction events)
outputs: health, mental health, material hardship; via eviction-event stress & displacement
effect_size: eviction is consistently associated with worse maternal/birth/mental-health outcomes; effect sizes large (e.g., increased adverse birth outcomes in 7/8 studies in scoping review)

title: Family food insufficiency, but not low family income, is positively associated with dysthymia and suicide symptoms in adolescents
input_modified: food insufficiency (food security as an input)
effect_size: ORs ~2-3x for dysthymia/suicidal symptoms among food-insufficient adolescents, independent of income

title: School Nutrition Policies and Associations With Academic Outcomes: A Comprehensive Summary
effect_size: 33 studies: most report positive or neutral academic associations; equity-oriented studies find larger gains for low-income/racial-minority students

title: The Effects of Focused Deterrence Strategies on Crime
venue: Journal of Research in Crime and Delinquency (Braga et al.)
input_modified: group- and individual-focused deterrence policing programs
effect_size: meta-analysis of 11 studies: overall statistically significant, MEDIUM-sized crime reduction (d ≈ 0.3-0.4), but strongest effects from weakest designs

title: Environmental Policy as Social Policy? The Impact of Childhood Lead Exposure on Crime
venue: The B.E. Journal of Economic Analysis & Policy (Reyes)
effect_size: elasticity of violent crime w.r.t. childhood lead exposure ≈ 0.8 — i.e., large: the lead removal explains a substantial share of 1990s violent-crime decline; murder/property effects less clear

title: Neighborhoods and Violent Crime: A Multilevel Study of Collective Efficacy
input_modified: neighborhood collective efficacy (social cohesion + willingness to intervene)
effect_size: collective efficacy explains a substantial share (measured between-neighborhood variation reduced violence across 343 Chicago neighborhoods; strong inverse association even adjusting for concentration of disadvantage, mixed land use, density)

title: Summer jobs reduce violence among disadvantaged youth
input_modified: summer jobs program (One Summer Chicago Plus)
effect_size: 43% reduction in violent-crime arrests (3.95 fewer arrests per 100 youth); null on property/drug crime

title: How Effective Are Mentoring Programs for Youth? A Systematic Assessment of the Evidence
venue: Psychological Science in the Public Interest (DuBois et al.)
outputs: delinquency, aggression, school engagement, psychosocial functioning
effect_size: meta-analytic mean effect d ≈ 0.18-0.21 (small), stronger where program quality + youth needs are matched; Big-Brothers-Big-Sisters style effects similar

title: Impact of Mental Health Act deinstitutionalization on crime rate of people with schizophrenia (Korea)
outputs: crime rates among people with schizophrenia
effect_size: DiD: deinstitutionalization associated with increases in overall crime & violence among psychiatric patients (not murders); schizophrenia group's baseline murder/archon risk 5x/11x general population
effect_direction: reducing beds increased some crime rates

title: Hospital-based violence intervention programs (HVIPs) — pediatric gun violence
venue: Handbook of Anger, Aggression, and Violence (2022)
effect_size: small single-site studies suggest lower reinjury/arrest; effect sizes typically d ≈ 0.1–0.3, high heterogeneity, low causal strength

title: The Effects of School Spending on Educational and Economic Outcomes (Jackson, Johnson, Persico)
outputs: years of education, adult wages, adult poverty
effect_size: 10% per-pupil spending increase ALL 12 YEARS → +0.31 years of education, +7% adult wages, -3.2 pp adult poverty (larger for low-income children); test scores up 0.05-0.2 SD per year of higher spending in earlier work
basis_of_estimate: school finance reform IV / event study

title: Measuring the Impacts of Teachers II: Teacher Value-Added and Student Outcomes in Adulthood
outputs: college attendance, earnings, teen pregnancy, 401(k) saving
effect_size: improving a 1-SD-quality teacher for 1 year → student lifetime earnings up ≈1.5%; replacement of low-VA teacher by average VA worth ~$230k per classroom (annualized PV); smaller than class-size effects but persistent

title: How Does Your Kindergarten Classroom Affect Your Earnings? (Project STAR)
venue: Quarterly Journal of Economics (Chetty et al.)
outputs: earnings at age 27, college attendance, retirement savings
effect_size: 1 SD-knit classroom-quality increase → earnings +~3% in K-3 combined (impacts on test scores fade but adult outcomes persist); small class size ↑ college attendance but no significant age-27 earnings effect (imprecise)
effect_direction: positive on classroom quality; mixed for pure class size

title: Another One Rides the Bus: The Impact of School Transportation on Student Outcomes (Michigan)
effect_size: 0.5-1 pp ↑ attendance, 2-4 pp ↓ chronic absence for disadvantaged students at walking-distance cutoffs; no effect on achievement
effect_direction: positive on attendance; null on achievement

title: Transit Accessibility to Jobs and Employment Prospects for Welfare Recipients
effect_size: significant positive association between transit job accessibility and employment prospects, with magnitude modest (elasticities ~0.1-0.2 in empirical studies, spatial mismatch literature: Mismatch Index decline of 0.1 ↔ employment ↑ 1-3 pp)
basis_of_estimate: survey + administrative data on welfare recipients

title: Transit improvements and labor-market outcomes (Sanchez/other urban transit studies)
effect_size: typical magnitudes: improved transit access ↑ employment 5-15% for affected low-income neighborhoods in before-after studies; but mixed and heterogeneous

title: The Impacts of Neighborhoods on Intergenerational Mobility I: Childhood Exposure Effects (Chetty & Hendren)
input_modified: neighborhood / growing up in a better county
effect_size: each year of childhood spent in a better neighborhood → adult outcomes improve ~4% per year (linear exposure dose-response); e.g., 8 extra years in a 1-SD better area → +~30% earnings vs. baseline gap
basis_of_estimate: 7M families moving across CZs & counties, sibling + displacement shocks

title: The Effects of Exposure to Better Neighborhoods on Children: New Evidence from the Moving to Opportunity Experiment
input_modified: Moving to Opportunity voucher (young children vs. adolescents vs. adults)
effect_size: moving before age 13 ↑ college attendance +~2.4 pp, ↑ earnings ~31%, ↓ single parenthood ~4 pp; moving as adolescent slightly NEGATIVE
effect_direction: strong positive if moved young; negative if adolescent

title: Moving to Opportunity in Boston: Early Results (Katz, Kling, Liebman)
input_modified: housing voucher to move to low-poverty neighborhood
outputs: child behavior, mental health, parental stress, employment
effect_size: improved adult mental health and children's behavior in early years; null on employment/benefits reliance; ~0.2-0.4 SD effect on parent mental health

title: Material hardship and 529 college savings plan participation (SEED for Oklahoma Kids)
venue: Social Science Research (Huang, Nam, Sherraden et al.)
effect_size: CDA access → higher 529 participation (esp. mitigating material hardship); typical effect: ~+2-4 pp overall take-up; parental educational expectations up (d ≈ 0.1-0.3)

title: Social capital II: determinants of economic connectedness
effect_size: economic connectedness (share of high-SES friends) is ~2/3 the explanatory power of all measured factors combined — strongest single predictor of mobility; β ≈ 0.05-0.08 pp mobility increase per 1 pp higher connectedness

title: Impacts of Neighborhoods III/QJE — childhood exposure effects + opportunity Atlas
outputs: childhood adult income rank, incarceration, teen birth
effect_size: 1-SD better neighborhood (Atlas composite) → +~0.2-0.35 SD rank increase per ~10-14y of childhood exposure
basis_of_estimate: census tract income/rank + Chetty-Hendren exposure estimates

T1_food_housing.headline: SNAP/school-meals & housing-stability interventions: modest positive education effects when delivered early and consistently; eviction/public-housing removal ≈ null on achievement; food INSECURITY (the deficit side) is far more damaging than program receipt is helpful — asymmetric.
T1_food_housing.typical_effect_size: small (d ≈ 0.05-0.2 SD test scores) for positive delivery; deficit side (food insecurity/eviction) risks ORs 1.5-3 for mental health/behavior.
T1_food_housing.peak_leverage: preventing eviction + guaranteeing meals; NOT more vouchers in place (MTO vouchers for adolescents slightly negative).

T2_safety_care.headline: Safety interventions show the LARGEST single-input magnitudes: lead removal (elasticity of violent crime to lead ≈ 0.8), focused deterrence (d≈0.3-0.4), summer jobs (43% ↓ violence). Psychiatric-bed reduction raises some crime (Korea DiD).
T2_safety_care.typical_effect_size: medium to large on CRIME (the outcome most elastic to safety inputs), small to null on edu/health.
T2_safety_care.peak_leverage: childhood lead reduction, focused deterrence, summer jobs; mental-health capacity is protective but evidence thin.

T3_belonging.input: community cohesion / mentors / summer-jobs / social capital
T3_belonging.headline: Mentoring d ≈ 0.18 (small); collective efficacy explains big cross-neighborhood violence gaps; cross-class connectedness (Nature 2022) is the #1 predictor of upward mobility among all measured covariates.
T3_belonging.typical_effect_size: small at individual level (d≈0.1-0.25), large at community level (variance-explained style).
T3_belonging.peak_leverage: community-level structure (bridging ties) > individual-level mentor programs.

T4_edu_transport.input: money into schools, better teachers, transportation
T4_edu_transport.headline: School spending: the cleanest and DURABLE magnitude (7% wages / -3.2 pp poverty per 10% sustained spend). Teacher VA ≈ 1.5% lifetime earnings per 1-SD quality year. Transportation: attendance effects only.
T4_edu_transport.typical_effect_size: medium on long-run adult outcomes; smaller on contemporaneous test scores.
T4_edu_transport.peak_leverage: sustained (12-year) spending increases for low-income students; teacher replacement of bottom-decile VA; school buses only move attendance.

T5_choice_set.headline: Neighborhood effects per year of exposure: ~4% improvement in adult outcomes (Chetty-Hendren QJE 2018) and +31% adult earnings for pre-13 movers (MTO, AER 2016) — the LARGEST, most dose-responsive effect in the whole scan. CDAs: small but real.
T5_choice_set.typical_effect_size: large (earnings %, pp college) for neighborhood exposure; small (pp savings take-up) for asset policies.
T5_choice_set.peak_leverage: moving before age 13 to a mobility-friendly neighborhood; adolescent moves are net NEGATIVE → timing matters.

cross_cutting_summary: LARGEST effects come from T2 (safety) + T5 (neighborhood) interventions targeted at CHILDREN under age 13; adult- and adolescent-targeted versions of the same inputs give null or negative results.
MEDIUM effects: school spending (T4), deterrence policing (T2), lead removal (T2).
SMALLEST effects: vouchers-to-relax-constraints (T1), CDA take-up (T5), school transportation (T4), mentoring (T3).
Deficit side (food insecurity, eviction, lead exposure) shows bigger magnitudes than the program-delivery side — asymmetric losses; prevention >> remediation.
